title: What Are You Saying? -- Passing On What Was Said
desc: Reported speech, for the twenty minutes after a meeting that decide everything. Key expressions: minutes, action item, to recap, agenda, takeaway, to align, off the record, to circle back, chair, attendee, to touch base, word for word. Structure: he said and she told me, with the tense one step back in time.
vocab: Minutes
the written record of what was said and decided in a meeting
The minutes said the second phase had been approved on Tuesday.
Action item
a task given to a named person in a meeting
There were four action items and three of them were mine.
To recap
to summarize the main points again, briefly
Let me recap the three things he announced.
Agenda
the list of subjects for a meeting
The expansion was not on the agenda, and he raised it anyway.
Takeaway
the main point somebody should remember afterwards
The takeaway was that the dates had moved, not the budget.
To align
to make sure everybody understands and agrees on the same thing
We need ten minutes to align before we talk to the client.
Off the record
said in confidence, not to be repeated officially
He told me off the record that the date would move.
To circle back
to return to a subject later
He said he would circle back on the format next week.
Chair
the person who runs a meeting
The chair told us the agenda had changed that morning.
Attendee
a person who is present at a meeting
There were eleven attendees and only four of them spoke.
To touch base
to make brief contact with somebody to check something
I will touch base with the Santiago team before Friday.
Word for word
repeating exactly what somebody said, with no change
I am giving you his sentence word for word, not my reading of it.

paras: The most useful skill in a large company is not speaking well in the meeting. It is what happens in the twenty minutes afterwards, when somebody who was not an attendee calls you and asks what was decided.

Rosa missed the regional call, so a colleague gave her the three announcements. He said the second phase had been approved on Tuesday. He said the Lima office would open in June and not in March, which makes every date in her plan wrong. And he told her the director wanted one page from each account manager before the convention.

She asked the question that separates a professional from a rumour: did he say what should be on the page, or is that your reading of it? He had not said. When asked afterwards, the director told him that if he specified the format everybody would write the same thing. That sentence, repeated word for word, was more useful than the whole recap.

There are two rules here and they protect a reputation. First, separate what was said from what you concluded: she said the office would open in June is a fact, and this probably delays our targets is your opinion, which must be labelled as yours. Second, if you were not in the room, say so. Passing on half a sentence you heard off the record is the fastest way to become the person nobody tells anything to.
quiz: Why does the text say "he said the second phase had been approved" and not "has been"?
Because in reported speech the tense moves one step back.
What is the difference between said and told in this text?
Told is followed by a person; said is not.
What question does the text call the one that separates a professional from a rumour?
When exactly did he say it?
Did he say that, or is that your reading of it?
Who else was in the room?
What does the text say you must do if you were not in the room?
Repeat it anyway, since somebody has to.
Say that you were not there and that you are repeating what you were told.

tip.title: Reported Speech -- Statements
tip.intro: How English moves a sentence from the room where it was said to the room where you are. The tense takes one step back, and the reporting verb decides whether a person can follow it.
rows: The step back is grammatical, not factual. She has not stopped managing the accounts.
present perfect · past simple → past perfect
Both collapse into the same form.
"It has been approved." → "He said it had been approved."
will · can · may → would · could · might
The modals each move one step back too.
tell needs a person straight after it; say never takes one. This is where the Portuguese me disse causes the most damage.
now → then · today → that day · tomorrow → the next day · here → there
"I will send it tomorrow." → "She said she would send it the next day."
tip.note: That is optional and leaving it out sounds more natural in speech. And the professional rule matters as much as the grammar: separate what was said from what you concluded, and say where the information came from when you were not in the room.

blanks: Hint: the original was I manage -- move it one step back
She said she managed thirty accounts.
Hint: the original was has approved -- one step back is the past perfect
He said the board had approved it.
Hint: will becomes would in reported speech
She said the office would open in June.
Hint: this reporting verb needs a person straight after it
He told me he could attend the convention.
Hint: the original was I sent yesterday -- one step back
She said she had sent the proposal the day before.
He said he would send it
Hint: tomorrow does not survive in reported speech
He said he would send it the next day.

order.intro: Listen to the summary of the debrief call, then put the steps in the correct order.
items: Julio tells Rosa that she missed the regional call and that there were three announcements.
He explains that the director said the second phase had been approved on Tuesday.
Rosa asks about the dates, and Julio answers that the Lima office would open in June instead of March.
Rosa says the dates in her own plan are now wrong and that she will correct them.
Julio adds the third point about the one page and admits that he does not know what should be on it.

speech: He said the second phase had been approved on Tuesday.
She said the office would open in June, not in March.
He told me he could not attend the convention.
That is my reading of it, not his words.
I was not on the call, so I am repeating what I was told.

quiz.intro: A colleague missed the call and a client has heard a rumour. Choose the best thing to say.
items: You want to report what the director announced. You say:
He said me that the second phase had been approved.
He told me that the second phase had been approved.
He told that the second phase had been approved.
The original sentence was "the office will open in June". You report:
She said the office will open in June.
She said the office would open in June.
She said the office opens in June.
The original was "I can attend the convention". You report:
He said he can attend the convention.
He told he could attend the convention.
He said he could attend the convention.
You want to make clear that the conclusion is yours and not the director's. You say:
That is my reading of it, not his words.
He said that our targets will move.
Everybody knows the targets are moving.
A client asks about something you heard second hand. The most professional answer is:
The director said the dates have moved, definitely.
I was not on the call, so I am repeating what I was told.
I cannot talk about that.

think: Take a real meeting from your own week and record the debrief, in about ninety seconds, for a colleague who was not there. Report three things that were said, using said and told correctly and moving each tense one step back. Then say one thing that was not said, and finish with one conclusion of your own, clearly labelled as yours.
survival: He said the second phase had been approved on Tuesday.
She said the office would open in June, not in March.
He told me he could not attend the convention.
That is my reading of it, not his words.
I was not on the call, so I am repeating what I was told.
